desc:
Given an array nums of non-negative integers and an integer target, find the length of the longest contiguous subarray whose bitwise XOR equals target. If no subarray qualifies, return 0.

nums = [3, 1, 2, 7, 4], target = 7
the block [3, 1, 2, 7] has XOR 7 (the single element [7] also does, but is shorter)
result = 4
hints: The XOR of a block is the XOR of two prefix values. Which two prefix positions give the longest block for a fixed end?
For an ending position j you need an earlier prefix with value px[j] ^ target, and to make the block as long as possible you want the earliest such prefix.
Store only the first index at which each prefix XOR value occurs (value 0 at index 0). Do not overwrite it when the value repeats. For each j, look up px[j] ^ target and update the best length.
editorial: With prefix XORs px[0..n], the block between prefixes i < j has XOR px[i] ^ px[j]. We want px[i] ^ px[j] = target with j - i maximal. For a fixed j the partner value is px[j] ^ target, and among all prefixes holding that value the smallest i gives the longest block.

So keep a dictionary of the first occurrence of each prefix XOR. While scanning, look up the partner for the current prefix first, then store the current prefix only if it is new (the lookup first matters when target = 0, where the partner is the prefix itself and must come from an earlier position). O(n) time, O(n) space. The contrasting problem, counting such blocks, stores a count per value instead of the first index.
